Ugandan Electric Utilities Face Widespread Disruption Amid Ongoing Workers' Strike

Kampala—A nationwide strike by electric utility workers in Uganda has entered its third day, causing unprecedented operational disruption across the country’s electric utilities sector. The walkout, which began early Monday morning, has affected critical transmission and distribution services, with Uganda Electricity Transmission Co Ltd among the key companies currently impacted.

The industrial action follows a deadlock in wage negotiations between the National Union of Energy Workers and electric utility employers. Union leaders claim that workers have faced stagnant pay and increasingly difficult working conditions since last year’s regulatory changes, which they argue have placed additional strain on the workforce. “The cost of living has risen sharply, but our members’ salaries have not kept pace,” said union secretary Paul Mutebi at a press conference in Kampala. “We are left with no option but to withhold our labor until our concerns are addressed.”

As of Wednesday afternoon, Uganda Electricity Transmission Co Ltd reported that more than 60 percent of its technical workforce had joined the walkout. According to company spokesperson Miriam Namutebi, the situation has forced the postponement of routine maintenance activities and delayed scheduled upgrades on the national grid. “We are prioritizing emergency repairs to prevent system failures, but our capacity is severely limited at this time,” she said.

Smaller regional operators, including the privately-owned Nile Power Associates, have also seen operations curtailed, with reports of delayed fault response and reduced grid monitoring capabilities. A statement from the Uganda Electric Utilities Association estimated that system reliability had dropped by approximately 30 percent since the strike began, citing increased frequency of interruptions and slower restoration times. “The continuity of reliable power transmission is at risk if this impasse is not swiftly resolved,” warned association chairperson James Okello.

Energy analyst Sarah Kigozi noted that while Uganda’s electric utilities have weathered localized labor disputes before, the current strike is notable for its scale and coordination. “The transmission network is highly dependent on skilled technical staff. Prolonged absenteeism could result in more severe grid instability, especially if critical faults go unaddressed,” Kigozi explained.

Government officials have called for renewed dialogue between union representatives and management, but no breakthrough has been reported so far. In the meantime, electric utility operators are urging customers to conserve electricity and to report outages promptly, while contingency teams work to maintain essential services.

As negotiations continue, industry leaders are warning that the ongoing strike could have lasting effects on Uganda’s electric utilities sector if a resolution is not reached soon.
